episodes.169325: Despite an early onset to the year's monsoon season and significant June rainfall totals, flash flooding and debris flow had not been reported across the largest burn scar in New Mexico likely thanks to steady, stratiform rain that had been occurring since mid-June. However, a more traditional monsoon pattern finally set up on July 1, 2022 as the high pressure to the east of New Mexico allowed for a deep plume of monsoonal moisture. Thunderstorms that developed over the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn area were now more convective and prone to producing heavy rainfall rates. This caused the most significant flash flooding so far of the season as multiple reports of flooding and debris flow across the burn scar were received. This prompted evacuations and road closures across western Mora and San Miguel counties.
episodes.169382: As deep layer moisture increased ahead of an approaching cold front on July 1, 2022, low level convergence on the leading edge of moisture advection coincided with lift associated with the right entrance region of a 95KT upper jet. The result was multiple clusters of thunderstorms moving across the southern half of central PA through the afternoon, several of which produced isolated areas of straight line wind damage. Another line of convection developed closer to the cold front during the evening in NW Pennsylvania and moved southeastward, producing isolated straight line wind damage until about 1:00 AM EDT on July 2. The downburst potential was enhanced by a layer of dry air in the environment above 750 hPa, which resulted in DCAPE values of 1200-1300 J/kg through the day and into the evening hours.

episodes.170318: A surface cold front drifted southeastward across northern Indiana, southeast Lower Michigan, southern Ontario, and into northwest Ohio during the afternoon through early evening of the 1st. Simultaneously, a pre-frontal surface trough axis in the warm sector moved generally eastward across northern Ohio and western Lake Erie toward eastern Lake Erie and northwest Pennsylvania. Low-level convergence and ascent along the pre-frontal trough axis acted as a focus for the development of multicellular showers and thunderstorms amidst weak to moderate MUCAPE, moderate DCAPE, and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. One of the multicell thunderstorms produced isolated straight-line wind damage in Erie County, Pennsylvania.
episodes.170319: A surface cold front drifted southeastward across northern Indiana, southeast Lower Michigan, southern Ontario, and into northwest Ohio during the afternoon through early evening of the 1st. Low-level convergence and ascent along the pre-frontal trough axis acted as a focus for the development of multicellular showers and thunderstorms amidst weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong DCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively. Some of the multicell storms produced isolated straight-line wind damage.

Low-level convergence and ascent along the pre-frontal trough axis acted as a focus for the development of multicellular showers and thunderstorms over western and central Lake Erie, and vicinity. episodes.172275: Spring snowmelt, record April precipitation and frequent May rain events led to strong hydrologic responses within the Rainy Lake basin. These high lake levels led to significant damage to homes and businesses along the shoreline along with docks and other related structures. Additionally, some roads were covered in water with one being temporarily raised to maintain access to a few resorts. In addition to the costs of the damage itself, many resorts in the area suffered from lost revenue by having to close during the beginning of peak tourist season in the area.

Above normal snowfall for the 2021-2022 season was observed across northern portions of Koochiching and St. Louis counties and much of that remained on the ground into April. Heavy rainfall then fell on top of that above normal snowpack at the end of April and sent abnormally high amounts of runoff into the Rainy River Basin leading to rises on Rainy Lake. International Falls experienced their wettest April on record, helping to set the stage for the flooding. By June 15th, the level of Rainy Lake reached 1113.2 feet which was 22 inches above the 2014 peak level and 2.5 inches above the all-time record set in 1950. Having crested and setting a new all-time high, the lake level fell over the remainder of the month to 1112.4 feet (13 inches above 2014 peak and slightly below the 1950 record) by the start of July having fallen 11 inches since peaking on June 15. As for Namakan Lake and Kabetogama Lake, they crested at 1122.4 feet (22 inches above the 2014 peak and 6 inches below the record 1916 peak) June 1st and then fell over the remainder of June reaching 1119.6 feet (below the 2014 peak) by July 1st, having fallen 37 inches since peaking on June 1st. The high lake levels led to extensive damage to properties adjacent to the water along with damage to docks and other infrastructure. Lake levels would continue to fall over the first two weeks of July with the Flood Warning being canceled on July 11th as Namakan and Kabetogama Lakes had returned to their normal regulated levels. Levels on Rainy Lake remained above normal at this time, but were receding and the threat for additional flooding had ended. State and Federal disasters were declared for the event with millions of dollars in infrastructure damage and property loss.

The James River at Columbia reached the July peak early in the month, with a slow decrease for the rest of the month. The river fell below the moderate stage on the 30th.

The James River at Stratford reached a July peak of 17.84 feet on the 8th, with a slow decrease for the rest of the month. On Friday, July 22, an 11 year old girl was rescued from the James River after accidentally falling into the water.

On Friday, July 22nd, a 13-year-old girl was swept downstream while swimming in the James River near Frankfort. The search was postponed around 11:30 p.m. Friday due to the dangers of the current and the inability to see in the dark. The girl's body was found around 9:25 a.m. on Saturday.

Rainfall totals of 2 to 3 inches across southern portions of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar caused significant flash flooding and debris flow. Widespread flooding was observed along Highway 105 with drainages well out of their banks. A barn along Highway 105 was also flooded. This forced the closure of the highway for several hours on July 1st. County Road A4B was also flooded with debris flow across the roadway. Damages are estimated.
Trees blew down near the intersection of US-15 James Madison Highway and VA-686 Ingram Drive.
A flood wave around 3 feet or higher passed through Pleasant Creek within Captitol Reef National Park. The flood wave was associated with heavy rainfall in close vicinity to the creek.
Heavy rain rates that occurred over a 30 minute timeframe resulted in the collapse of a roof along the 400 block of Highway 11 in Ellisville.
Several large trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds on Cumberland Gap Road. One tree fell on a utility line and snapped a utility pole.
Pea sized hail accompanied the storm.

Multiple trees downed about two-miles WSW of North East.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree onto a house on Amelia Avenue.
Numerous trees downed in Fremont. Four of these trees fell onto houses and one fell onto a car. A mesonet station in Fremont recorded a peak convective gust of 61 mph.
A tractor trailer was blown-over by strong convective wind gusts about 1.2 miles-WNW of downtown Fremont. Business' signs were also damaged in the area.

Structural damage occurred at the Sandusky County Fairgrounds in Fremont. Three buildings had metal siding damaged. One of these buildings had its large metal door blown-in and half of its roof torn off. A barricade was blown into a car and injured the driver.

The Utah Department of Transportation I-80 at MP 107 mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 71 mph. The wind gust was associated with microburst outflow winds from a nearby thunderstorm.
A couple trees were blown down along Montague Drive by thunderstorm winds.
A wind gust of 58 mph was measured by the PleasantValley - Agrimet PLVU sensor as a shower moved over the site during the late afternoon.

Over three inches of rain fell in an hour over Ellsworth Air Force Base and parts of Box Elder. Runoff from the heavy rain flooded streets, homes, and businesses. Several streets were flooded on Ellsworth Air Force Base and throughout northern and eastern portions of Box Elder. At least 50 mobile homes were surrounded by water and ten to 15 homes were flooded with water up to six feet deep, mostly along the east side of North Ellsworth Road. Several businesses reported that their parking lots were flooded.

Over three inches of rain fell in an hour over Ellsworth Air Force Base and parts of Box Elder.  Runoff from heavy rain flooded streets, homes, and businesses. Several streets were flooded on Ellsworth Air Force Base, Antelope Ridge, and throughout northern and eastern portions of Box Elder.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down multiple trees in the Town of Delaware.
Lightning struck a house in the 23600 block of White Peach Court, causing a fire in the basement that displaced 2 residents and resulted in about $15,000 in damage.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down multiple trees in Bethel.

Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 1 hour caused urban washes to flow over roadways from midtown to southeast Tucson. One person was washed downstream in the Columbus Wash near Blacklidge Dr. but was able to get themselves to safety. A young woman was rescued from her car which was stuck in Arcadia Wash near Pima and Rosemont. Kolb Rd. was closed between Irvington and Valencia while Irvington Rd. was closed due to flooding at the Atterbury Wash.
Canopy tents were collapsed and damaged at a Downtown Festival in Houlton. Multiple trees were also reported down across the town. Wind gusts were estimated at up to 60 mph. The time is estimated.

Thunderstorm downburst winds snapped or uprooted trees from Rush County Fairgrounds across northern and northeastern portions of Rushville.  Falling trees damaged 4 vehicles and 2 homes.  Winds downed tents, trailers awnings and tables at the Rush County Fair, leading to flying debris that possibly caused injuries.  The top half of a communication tower was bent over and onto the Rushville Police Department.  Another tree was downed at 815 East 11th Street.
A couple trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
A wind gust of 65 mph was recorded by the Lucin2 UPR weather sensor in association with outflow winds due to a nearby shower.
